title: Blessed is Ram Das
hook: the minstrels Satta and Balvand praise the Gurus' light passing on (Ramkali ki Var, ang 968)
tomorrow: I never knew what You did

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, and your line: many names, one lord. Did you hear someone name God in other words, and listen for the One? Today, a song by two musicians about one light in many lamps. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Open the Guru Granth Sahib and you find the Gurus' hymns, and the words of saints the Gurus gathered. But a few pages come from people who were in the room with the Gurus. Among them, tradition says, were two musicians of the Guru's court, Satta and Balvand, who played the rabab and sang. They watched the line of Gurus pass from one to the next, and they wrote about it the way musicians would: in a ballad, a var. Today, one line from it rings out: blessed is Ram Das.
screen: `HYMNS BY GURUS AND SAINTS.` → `AND TWO MUSICIANS IN THE ROOM.` → `A BALLAD, A VAR.`

segments.voice: Their var sits in Raag Ramkali, on Angs nine sixty-six to nine sixty-eight. It's short, and it tells one story: Guru Nanak's light passing to Guru Angad, then to Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan. The line everyone remembers comes early, in a stanza about Guru Angad. In paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the Master has only changed the body. Jot ohaa, jugat saae. One light, one way. That single phrase holds the Sikh understanding of the ten Gurus: not ten different teachers, but one light passing from lamp to lamp. Then, on Ang nine sixty-eight, the stanza for the fourth Guru opens: dhan dhan Raam Daas gur. In paraphrase: blessed, blessed is Guru Ram Das; the One who made you has also adorned you. And the same stanza names him as one with those before him: you are Nanak, you are Lehna, you are Amar Das. Why does this matter? Because the var is a witness. It isn't a theologian explaining succession. It's two singers, standing close enough to see it, saying: we watched the same light move. Sikhs still sing their var, and the phrase jot ohaa jugat saae is often quoted when people speak of the Gurus as one. The musicians' own names, Satta and Balvand, are in the Guru Granth Sahib forever. The people who carried the tune are kept in the book.
screen: `TWO MINSTRELS, ONE BALLAD.` · `ONE LIGHT, ONE WAY, A NEW BODY.` · `BLESSED, BLESSED IS RAM DAS.` · `WITNESSES, KEPT IN THE BOOK.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT PASSES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise someone's teacher. Sit and think of a person you admire. Then ask: who taught them? A parent, a coach, a mentor, a grandmother, a book. Picture the light passing from that teacher to the person you admire, and maybe from them to you. Silently say, blessed is the one who taught them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in thanks for that line of teachers. The bell holds the time.
Jot, light: the musicians Satta and Balvand's ballad about the fourth Guru says the jot is the same, the way is the same, and only the body changes.
Your line: the light passes on. Today, tell someone about a teacher who shaped you, or thank a teacher who shaped someone you love. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 669 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I NEVER KNEW WHAT YOU DID.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Satta and Balvand's var in kirtan, and quote its phrase about the same light and the same way when speaking of the ten Gurus as one.

match.prompt: the minstrels' var — tap the pairs.
pairs: court musicians who wrote the var

myth: every hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib was written by a Guru
the Gurus also included saints, and musicians like Satta and Balvand.
the var says the light stays the same while the body changes
jot ohaa jugat saae: one light, one way, a new body.

fork.setup: you're one of the Gurus' musicians, watching the leadership pass to a new Guru. what does the var say you saw?
options: the same light in a new body.
fork.reveal: the light is the same, the way is the same; only the body changed. Sikhs still speak of the Gurus as one light.

original.note: Gurmukhi: light; the var says the jot, the light, passed unchanged from Guru to Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: it's a song praising one Guru.
what it means: it's a witness that one light passed through each Guru.
what a scholar hears: Satta and Balvand's Ramkali var (Ang 966–968) states the Gurus' single light in the words of musicians who, tradition says, served at the Guru's court.

notes: Editor review (y2 669-687): cut the unsourced 'eight stanzas' count and 'almost every hymn' claim; replaced the pool-digging/throne images (not confirmed in this stanza) with the stanza's 'you are Nanak, you are Lehna, you are Amar Das' (confirm, Ang 968); softened 'whenever' and the 'earliest statement, eyewitness' trapdoor.
Var structure (eight pauris; Nanak to Arjan) and Ang range 966–968: confirm.
'jot ohaa jugat saae sahi kaaiaa pher palateeai' placed in the stanza about Guru Angad, Ang 966: confirm.
'dhan dhan raam daas gur jin siriaa tinai savaariaa' paraphrased; the reference to digging the pool and sitting on Nanak's throne: confirm these images are in this stanza.
The tradition of a quarrel between the musicians and Guru Arjan is left out deliberately.
